Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:

Content:
It can be shown that the random variable [MATH: X,] defined as
[MATH: X = \dfrac{W_1/\nu_1}{W_2/\nu_2}]
follows a two-parameter probability distribution called an [MATH: \boldsymbol F]-distribution. We denote this as follows:

Content:
[MATH: X\sim F(\nu_1, \nu_2)]

Content:

Since an [MATH: F]-distribution is a ratio of chi-square random variables with support [MATH: x > 0,] the support of [MATH: f(x)] is also [MATH: x > 0.]

Content:
The [MATH: F]-distribution is sometimes called Fisher's [MATH: \boldsymbol F]-distribution after the British statistician Sir Ronald Fisher.

Item 6 — Tutorial: The Reciprocal Property

Content:
Earlier, we saw that if [MATH: W_1] and [MATH: W_2] are independent chi-square random variables with [MATH: \nu_1] and [MATH: \nu_2] degrees of freedom, respectively.
[MATH: W_1\sim \chi(\nu_1), \qquad W_2\sim \chi(\nu_2)]

Content:
then, we have
[MATH: X = \dfrac{W_1/\nu_1}{W_2/\nu_2} \sim F(\nu_1, \nu_2).]

Content:
Naturally, if the ratio [MATH: (W_1/\nu_1)/(W_2/\nu_2)] follows a f-distribution, then [MATH: (W_2/\nu_2)/(W_1/\nu_1)] follows a f-distribution, too.

Content:
[MATH: Y = \dfrac{1}{X} = \dfrac{W_2/\nu_2}{W_1/\nu_1} \sim F(\nu_2, \nu_1)]

Content:
It follows then that
[MATH: P(X\geq c) + P\left(Y\geq\dfrac1c\right) = 1]

Content:
The diagram below shows a sketch of the probability density functions [MATH: f_X(x)] and [MATH: f_Y(y)] of the random variables [MATH: X] and [MATH: Y.] The sum of the two shaded areas equals [MATH: 1.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b710e700d2b51e5caac6c9ae31014530]

Content:

Content:
[MATH: P(X\geq c) = p.]

Content:
Therefore, by rearranging the inequality in the parentheses, we have

Content:
[MATH: P\left(\dfrac1X\leq \dfrac1c\right) = p.]
In other words,
[MATH: P\left(Y\leq \dfrac1c\right) = p.]
Using the complement, we have
[MATH: P\left(Y\geq \dfrac1c\right) = 1-p.]
Therefore, we conclude
[MATH: P(X ≥ c) + P(Y ≥ (1)/(c)) = p + (1 − p) = 1.]

Content:
Let's see how the reciprocal property can be used to find probabilities.
